query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An optimized AlCoCrFeNi‐based high-entropy alloy with a tailored composition that promotes the formation of a stable, protective oxide scale (e.g., alumina and/or chromia) will show significantly improved tribo-corrosion resistance under elevated temperature and sliding (wear) conditions compared to conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy or conventional structural alloy used in high-temperature corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Modify the HEA composition by fine-tuning the relative amounts of elements such as Al and Cr to enhance the formation of compact, self-healing protective oxide layers during high-temperature exposure, using advanced alloy synthesis techniques.
generation.conditions: Simulated extreme environments featuring elevated temperatures (e.g., 500–800°C) combined with corrosive and wear-inducing sliding conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a dual-phase microstructure that supports the formation and retention of protective oxide scales on the material surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the tailored alloy facilitates the in situ formation of a protective oxide layer (e.g., alumina or chromia) that serves as a diffusion barrier. This layer, together with a stable underlying microstructure, minimizes the combined effect of mechanical wear and corrosive attack (tribo-corrosion), thereby retarding material degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in both the wear and corrosion rates, evidenced by lower mass loss and improved surface integrity under testing conditions, when compared to conventional alloys.
generation.baseline: The performance of standard structural alloys or conventional (untailored) HEAs under equivalent high-temperature, corrosive sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under controlled laboratory conditions simulating extreme environments (500–800°C with corrosive sliding) and may not extend to environments with substantially different stressors or loading regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal compositional window and exact magnitude of improvement in degradation resistance remain uncertain. Further experiments are required to define the composition-performance relationship and to quantify the benefit in tribo-corrosion resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of specimens: one of the tailored AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA with optimized Al and Cr concentrations, and a control sample of either a conventional structural alloy or an untailored HEA. Subject both to a tribo-corrosion test in a high-temperature chamber (500–800°C) where the samples are exposed to simultaneous sliding wear and a corrosive environment (e.g., a molten salt mixture or saline solution).
measurements: Wear rate (via profilometry and mass loss)
Corrosion rate (mass loss or electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored HEA does not display a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion rates, as well as fails to form or maintain a continuous protective oxide layer relative to the control under identical conditions, then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. The world economy is highly dependent on fossil fuels to meet persistent energy demands, which results in carbon emissions and negative environmental impacts. This is driving the global search for sustainable and alternative energy sources [ [1] ], solar energy being one of the most viable and clean options [ [2] ]. The global capacity for concentrating solar power (CSP) systems has increased fifteen-fold over the last two decades [ [3] ]. The solar power conversion systems in CSP operate with advanced fluids above 400 °C [ [4] ], using molten salts such as solar salt [ [5] ], Hitec salt [ [6] ], and MgNaK chlorides [ [7] ]. In particular, the ternary MgNaK chloride (MgCl 2 -NaCl-KCl) eutectic salt mixture has high thermal stability and is more cost effective compared to other molten salts [ [8] , [9] ]. This allows CSP to operate at higher temperatures for higher efficiency of thermal-to-electrical energy conversion and reduces the cost of electricity. However, degradation of structural materials in a molten salt environment remains a critical concern in CSP systems [ [9] , [10] ].
